source.module_title: Adam Clarke's Commentary and critical notes on the Bible

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen31491" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31492" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31493" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31493" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31492" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31494" type="x-p"/> The prophet proceeds, by a variety of types and parables, to convince those of the captivity that their brethren who were left behind to sustain the miseries of a siege and the insults of a conqueror, would be in a much worse condition than they who were already settled in a foreign land. In the beginning of this chapter he foretells the approaching captivity of Judah by action instead of words, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.1-Eze.12.7">Eze 12:1-7</reference>. He predicts particularly the flight, capture, captivity, and sufferings of Zedekiah and his followers, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.8-Eze.12.16">Eze 12:8-16</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>. He is to eat his food with trembling and signs of terror, as an emblem of the consternation of the Jews when surrounded by their enemies, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.17-Eze.12.20">Eze 12:17-20</reference>; and then he answers the objections and bywords of scoffers and infidels, who either disbelieved his threatening or supposed the accomplishment of them very distant, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.21-Eze.12.28">Eze 12:21-28</reference>. Josephus (Antiq. 11:10) tells us that Zedekiah thought the prophecy of Ezekiel in the thirteenth verse inconsistent with that of Jeremiah, (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">Jer 34:3</reference>), and resolved to believe neither. Both, however, were literary fulfilled; and the event convinced him that they were not irreconcilable. Thus, blinded by infidelity, sinners rush on to that destruction against which they are sufficiently warned.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31495" type="x-p"/> Which have eyes to see, and see not - It is not want of grace that brings them to destruction. They have eyes to see, but they will not use them. No man is lost because he had not sufficient grace to save him, but because he abused that grace.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31497" type="x-p"/> Dig thou through the wall - This refers to the manner in which Zedekiah and his family would escape from the city. They escaped by night through a breach in the wall. See <reference osisRef="Jer.39.2-Jer.39.4">Jer 39:2-4</reference>; and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">2Kgs 25:4</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31498" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt cover thy face, that thou see not the ground - Referring to the blinding of Zedekiah: even the covering of the face might be intended to signify that in this way Zedekiah should be carried to Babylon on men's shoulders in some sort of palanquin, with a cloth tied over his eyes, because of the recent wounds made by extracting them. All the prophecies from this to the twentieth chapter are supposed to have been delivered in the sixth year of Zedekiah, five years before the taking of Jerusalem. How accurate the prediction! and how exactly fulfilled!

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31500" type="x-p"/> I will bring - him to Babylon - yet shall he not see it - Because Nebuchadnezzar caused him to have his eyes put out at Riblah. To Babylon he was carried in his blind state, and there he died. In saying, My net also will I spread upon him, there is probably a reference to an ancient manner of fighting. One, who was called the retiarius, had a small casting net, which if he could throw over his antagonist's head, he then dispatched him with his sword; if he missed his throw, he was obliged to run in order to get his net once more adjusted for another throw. In the mean time the other pursued him with all his speed to prevent this, and to dispatch him; hence he was called secutor: the first the netman, the second the pursuer.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31501" type="x-p"/> Eat thy bread with quaking - Assume the manner of a person who is every moment afraid of his life, who has nothing but a morsel of bread to eat, and a little water to drink. Thus signifying the siege, and the straits to which they should be reduced. See this explained, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.19">Eze 12:19</reference> (note).

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31502" type="x-p"/> The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth? - These are the words of the infidels and scoffers, who, because vengeance was not speedily executed on an evil work, set their heart to do iniquity. "These predictions either will not come in our days, or will wholly fail; why then should we disquiet ourselves about them?" Strange, that the very means used by the most gracious God to bring sinners to repentance, should be made by them the very instruments of their own destruction! See <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pet 3:4</reference>.
